claims.text: A hybrid machine-learned interatomic-potential workflow can accurately reproduce solid and liquid free energies near melting in multicomponent systems.
On-the-fly active learning can reduce the required ab initio training data to a modest set of molecular-dynamics snapshots from the solid and liquid phases.
Enhanced thermodynamic integration or path sampling with the machine-learned potential can be used to compute phase free energies.
The proposed workflow will retain vibrational entropy and anharmonic effects.
Built-in corrections can approximately retain electron–vibration coupling in the machine-learned workflow.
The intended operating range is approximately 0.8–1.2 times the melting temperature.
The method is intended for systems containing up to five components without dramatic phase separation caused by local chemical environments.
Locally resolved configurations and vibrational dynamics captured by the potential enable accurate estimation of force constants and anharmonic contributions.
Interpolation of the ab initio energy landscape by the machine-learned potential dramatically increases sampling speed.
The machine-learned potential preserves the key energy-surface features needed to calculate solid–liquid free-energy differences nearly as faithfully as explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
Solid–liquid free-energy differences, melting temperatures, and latent heats will agree within approximately ±10% of explicit ab initio results.
The proposed workflow will be approximately one order of magnitude faster than TOR-TILD.
The proposed workflow will be approximately two orders of magnitude faster than full ab initio molecular dynamics.
Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy calculations and TOR-TILD are computationally expensive, particularly for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The workflow is expected to remain reliable through quinary compositional complexity near melting.
Extreme compositions or temperatures far from melting may impair transferability of the potential.
Accuracy for electron–vibration coupling and very strong anharmonicity depends on the quality and scope of the training data.
